bib.title: When to Retrieve During Reasoning: Adaptive Retrieval for Large Reasoning Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "When to Retrieve During Reasoning: Adaptive Retrieval for Large Reasoning Models" (ReaLM-Retrieve). Dongxin Guo, Jikun Wu, Siu Ming Yiu. SIGIR '26 (Melbourne, July 2026), arXiv:2604.26649v1, 29 Apr 2026, doi 10.1145/3805712.3809722.

COVERAGE: I read the extraction up to about char 62,000 of 70,304 (12 pages). That covers every section, all tables and the limitations. The remaining ~8,000 chars are the reference list (I skimmed the entries up to [17], the rest unread). The paper has no appendices. I did not run the figure-captions script. Figure captions come from the text extraction. I have no page numbers, so locations are section numbers.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Claim: Retrieving fewer times, at uncertain reasoning steps, beat fixed-interval retrieval on both F1 and calls. This is the paper's "central finding".
  number: MuSiQue 71.2 F1 with 1.8 calls vs IRCoT 65.4 F1 with 3.4 calls (+5.8 F1, 47% fewer calls, 95% CI [4.2, 7.4]).
  setup: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, ColBERTv2 retriever, k=5, test sets of MuSiQue, HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA, 3 seeds, paired bootstrap with Bonferroni correction. The authors' own method is tuned on this setup.
  quote: "ReaLM-Retrieve achieves 71.2% F1 with 1.8 retrieval calls vs IRCoT's 65.4% F1 with 3.4 calls. This is a 5.8% absolute improvement with 47% fewer retrievals (95% CI: [4.2, 7.4], p< 0.01)."
  where: §6.1; Table 2.
- Claim: The timing signal matters. Replacing the uncertainty score with random triggering at the same call count costs 8.5 F1.
  number: 62.7 vs 71.2 F1, both at 1.8 calls. A fixed threshold costs -2.3 F1 and raises calls to 2.4.
  setup: MuSiQue, R1-32B, mean ± std over 3 seeds.
  quote: "RSUS→Random 62.7±1.2 1.8±0.1 -8.5 ∗∗" and "Random triggering degrades F1 by 8.5%, demonstrating that when to retrieve matters substantially."
  where: §6.3; Table 6.
- Claim: The gain over IRCoT grows with hop count.
  number: +3.2 (2-hop), +5.8 (3-hop), +8.4 (4-hop) F1 vs IRCoT.
  setup: MuSiQue, R1-32B.
  quote: "+3.2% F1 on 2-hop, +5.8% on 3-hop, and +8.4% on 4-hop questions vs IRCoT."
  where: §6.4; Figure 2.
- Claim: The method loses to single retrieve-then-read on some questions, mostly simple ones. The authors suggest complexity routing as a hybrid.
  number: 12% of questions (N=288).
  quote: "ReaLM-Retrieve also underperforms Single RAG on 12% of questions (N= 288), primarily simple 2-hop cases where early retrieval suffices, suggesting potential for hybrid approaches that detect question complexity before selecting retrieval strategy."
  where: §7.3.
- Claim: Efficiency. Per-call latency drops from 2.10 s (naive interleave) to 0.66 s. End-to-end latency is 14.1 s against IRCoT's 18.7 s. The gain comes from fewer calls, speculative caching (37% hit rate) and 73% context compression.
  number: 0.66 s vs 2.10 s per call; 14.1 s vs 12.4 s with no retrieval (+1.7 s) vs IRCoT +6.3 s.
  setup: MuSiQue, R1-32B, 8×A100, WARP retriever at 171 ms.
  quote: "ReaLM-Retrieve adds only 1.7 seconds latency over no-retrieval baseline (13.7% overhead) vs 6.3 seconds for IRCoT (51% overhead)."
  where: §6.2; Table 4.
  Caveat: Table 6 shows the three efficiency parts change F1 by only 0.2 to 0.4, so they are latency tools only.
- Claim: Cost and tokens. Chains are shorter with well-timed retrieval.
  number: 9,489 vs 11,284 tokens; $0.021 vs $0.025 per query, a 16% saving.
  setup: MuSiQue, R1-32B tokens priced at R1-671B output rates, $2.19/1M output tokens, input cost excluded.
  quote: "ReaLM-Retrieve reduces cost by 16% vs IRCoT (Table 5) while achieving 5.8% higher F1"
  where: §6.2; Table 5.
- Claim: It also beats Search-R1 (RL-trained search calls) with fewer calls.
  number: R1-671B MuSiQue 77.8 vs Search-R1 73.4 F1 (+4.4); R1-32B +4.4, 1.8 vs 2.4 calls; average F1 over the three sets 70.9 vs 67.8.
  quote: "With R1-671B, ReaLM-Retrieve achieves 77.8% F1 on MuSiQue, 4.4% above Search-R1 (95% CI: [3.0, 5.8], p< 0.01)"
  where: §6.1; Tables 2 and 3.
- Claim: It improves retrieval quality, not just call count.
  number: R@5 81.3 vs IRCoT 72.6 and Search-R1 74.1. "Useful%" is 82.4 vs 71.8 for IRCoT.
  setup: HotpotQA, judged against supporting-fact labels.
  quote: "Our method achieves 81.3% Recall@5, substantially higher than IRCoT (72.6%) and Search-R1 (74.1%)."
  where: §6.6; Table 7.
- Claim: When retrieval helps and when it hurts.
  number: 73% of successful retrievals fall at verification points; bridge facts give 41% of the gain over fixed-interval retrieval. Harmful cases: injection during exploratory strategy (31% of failures) and contradiction of grounded reasoning (18%).
  quote: "73% of successful retrievals occur at verification boundaries" and "retrieval harms reasoning when injected during exploratory strategy development (31% of failures)"
  where: §7.1.
- Claim: Failure analysis of 847 failed questions.
  number: Corpus gaps 43%, over-retrieval during exploration 31%, query formulation errors 26%.
  quote: "(1) Retrieval corpus gaps (43%) ... (2) Over-retrieval during exploration (31%) ... (3) Query formulation errors (26%)"
  where: §7.3.
- Claim: Transfer. The gain holds on QwQ-32B-Preview and when the policy is trained on HotpotQA.
  number: QwQ: 68.4 F1 with 1.7 calls vs IRCoT 63.2 with 3.2 calls. Trained on HotpotQA and tested on MuSiQue: 68.9 F1, 2.0 calls, 2.3 below in-domain.
  quote: "We achieve 68.4% F1 with 1.7 calls vs IRCoT's 63.2% with 3.2 calls"
  where: §6.7 and §6.8; Tables 8 and 9.
- Claim: The signal works without logprobs. RSUS = 0.40·verbalized confidence + 0.35·entity-coverage entropy + 0.25·consistency of 3 resampled continuations. For o1-class API models, a learned proxy replaces verbalized confidence.
  number: Proxy AUROC 0.71 vs 0.83 for true verbalized confidence. RSUS adds 8% overhead against 500–2000% for semantic entropy. Removing verbalized confidence costs -2.8 F1, entity entropy -2.1, consistency -0.9.
  quote: "achieving 0.71 AUROC against a held-out NaturalQuestions subset of 412 traces ..., substantially below the 0.83 AUROC of true verbalized confidence on open-weight models"
  where: §4.2 and §4.1 for weights (footnote 1); Table 6.
- Claim: The gate is a trained pipeline with four learned parts.
  number: The policy is a contextual bandit trained with REINFORCE, reward F1 − λ1·n_ret − λ2·t_latency, λ1 decayed 0.5 to 0.1 (curriculum), 50,000 steps, 19,938 training examples, 2,400 GPU-hours. Step segmenter: 94.2 F1, average step 127 tokens vs 23 for a sentence.
  where: §4.1, §4.3, §5.5, §7.5, §7.6.
- Claim: Phrasing queries as the information need beat phrasing them as the current reasoning step. Retrieved text is injected only at step boundaries.
  number: Removing query formulation costs -1.8 F1.
  quote: "queries formulated as the information need ... outperform queries formulated as the current reasoning step."
  where: §4.3, §4.4; Table 6.

LIMITS
- Concessions in §7.5:
  - Completion-only models do 2–3 F1 lower: "68.9% vs 71.2% F1 on MuSiQue for o1 vs R1".
  - The method is useless without a good corpus: "14% of out-of-domain retrievals return misleading information".
  - Quality degrades after 3 or more injections. Only 4.7% of test questions reach that regime.
  - Chains over 30K tokens make KV-cache memory prohibitive.
  - Real-time use is not covered. The paper says latency of 14.1 s "suits asynchronous workloads"; under 2 s "none of which we evaluate here".
- The segmenter's out-of-domain check uses only 15 traces per benchmark and a single annotator (§4.1, Table 1).
- Only multi-hop Wikipedia QA is tested (MuSiQue, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA). Nothing covers enterprise corpora, and there is no human judgement.
- The Self-RAG baseline uses Llama-2-13B, so the comparison is not like for like (acknowledged in §6.1). FLARE is marked as using token probabilities unavailable for R1-671B, so it is absent from the 671B rows.
- The paper's own results show a fixed-interval schedule is not the only alternative. Search-R1 sits between the two (2.4 calls, 66.8 F1).
- Internal inconsistencies I noticed:
  - §6.2 says "57% fewer retrieval calls overall", while 1.8 vs 4.2 is 57% against naive interleave. The 47% figure is against IRCoT.
  - The text cites "Table 7" for the o1 vs R1 gap, but Table 7 is retrieval quality, and I found no o1 table in the extraction. The 68.9 figure also equals the Table 9 transfer F1, so treat the o1 number as unverified.
  - The abstract's "10.1% over standard RAG" is an absolute-F1 average: 70.9 vs 60.8 in Table 2.
- The latency figure comes from a research setup (8×A100, WARP at 171 ms), not a production service.
- Authors' affiliations include a company (Brain Investing Limited). The code is not mentioned in the portion I read.

BUILDS ON
- IRCoT (Trivedi et al.; cited as [31]; retrieve after each sentence).
- FLARE (Jiang et al., EMNLP 2023; token-probability trigger).
- DRAGIN (attention-entropy trigger; [27]).
- Self-RAG (Asai et al., ICLR 2024).
- Adaptive-RAG (Jeong et al., NAACL 2024; query-complexity routing).
- Open-RAG (Islam et al., Findings of EMNLP 2024).
- REPLUG ([26]).
- Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025, COLM).
- ReARTeR ([28], SIGIR 2025).
- Dynamic Search-R1 / Cost-Aware Retrieval-Augmentation Reasoning Models with Adaptive Retrieval Depth (Hashemi et al., WWW 2026; concurrent, a different axis: depth vs timing).
- DeepSeek-R1 (Nature 2025).
- Uncertainty signals: semantic entropy (Kuhn et al., ICLR 2023), verbalized confidence ([29]), self-consistency (Wang, [32]), Lin et al. pairwise-similarity uncertainty ([19]), TRAQ ([18]).
- Retrieval stack: ColBERTv2, PLAID, WARP, vLLM.
- Policy training: REINFORCE (Williams, [34]).

CODE: none in the paper. Two pieces are worth keeping verbatim:
- The verbalized-confidence prompt (§4.2): "Given the reasoning so far, rate your confidence that the current conclusion is factually correct on a scale of 0-100, where 0 means completely uncertain and 100 means absolutely certain. Respond with only a number:"
- The injection format (§4.4): a `<retrieved>…</retrieved>` block plus the continuation prompt "Continue your reasoning, using this evidence if relevant."

FIGURES
- Fig. 1: problem, four-stage pipeline (segment, detect RSUS, policy, integrate) and the MuSiQue F1-vs-calls scatter. It is the fastest picture of retrieve-once vs retrieve-at-gaps.
- Fig. 2: F1 by hop count (2, 3, 4) for four systems. It shows the gap widening with difficulty. The y-axis starts at 48.
- Fig. 3: histogram of retrieval position within the chain, successful vs failed questions. Successful runs cluster near 20% and 50%.
- Candidate for the note: Table 4, the calls, latency, per-call and F1/call comparison, as a small table.

FIT TO THE NOTES (greps of notes/ and references.md)
- Best home: `/Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/02-rag-retrieval/notes/07-rag-in-production.md`, in the "router row" passage (lines ~342-344). That passage already covers RAGate, Adaptive-RAG, Probing-RAG, Skill-RAG and a DRAGIN mention, and it has a measured-gate pattern with caveats.
- No note or references row cites arXiv:2604.26649 or Guo. So this is new, not a sharpens.
- Closest existing claims, which this extends:
  - 07 says gates cut cost. The Skill-RAG paragraph says "The probes need white-box hidden states ... so they cannot gate a hosted API model."
  - Guo supplies the contrast: a gate built only from output text (verbalized confidence, entity coverage, resampling) that works on both open and API reasoning models, with the proxy's 0.71 AUROC as the API-model cost.
  - It is also a gate that fires mid-chain at step boundaries, which the existing paragraph does not cover.
  - It adds ablation evidence that timing, not just call count, carries the gain (random trigger at equal calls: -8.5 F1).
- Possible secondary spots: `11-retrieval-improvements.md` (line ~245, "AgentIR: when the caller is an agent, its reasoning is the free expansion"; same reasoning-model theme) and `01-rag-pipeline.md` (line ~91, the "Adaptive" intent-classifier row; line ~438, agentic RAG as ReAct).
- Suggested references row: Guo, Wu & Yiu, SIGIR 2026, arXiv:2604.26649, with the setup (R1-Distill-32B, MuSiQue, ColBERTv2) and the caveats above (author-tuned, Wikipedia multi-hop only, 14.1 s latency, o1 figure unverified).

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions. The extraction is clean text with minor spacing faults (for example "contextbeforereasoning") and garbled chart axes (Figure 1c, Figure 2 numbers).
- The extraction has no page numbers, so I gave section locations.
- The Figure 2 numbers are uncertain because the chart values are interleaved in the text, so I used only the values stated in the prose.
